Responses protocol, streaming, and failures

Responses wire contract: collaboration transport, response ids, item replay, stream terminals, failure classes, retry budgets, capacity, and request hardening.

About 17 min read · 8 sections

On this page
01 Collaboration tool transport and arguments 02 Response ids, cache affinity, and turn state 03 Service tiers on Responses upstreams 04 Replayed items and turn terminals 05 Streaming, reasoning summaries, and heartbeats 06 Provider failures and retry budgets 07 Capacity and supported surface 08 WebSocket refusals, internal fields, and control items

Part of Responses support: how one Responses request travels. Tool declarations and tool-call rules live on Responses tools across routes, and what each inference route does with a request lives on Responses provider adapters and images.

Collaboration tool transport and arguments

Collaboration tool transport. Before forwarding to a translated Responses provider, the gateway removes the optional encrypted JSON Schema marker only from parameters.properties.message on the exact collaboration namespace function tools spawn_agent, send_message, and followup_task. Those caller- executed message arguments therefore remain plaintext for a provider that cannot decrypt Codex transport ciphertext. On the Codex subscription route only, the reserved collaboration namespace is also given a collision-free gateway_collaboration wire alias (with underscores appended when needed) in top-level and additional_tools declarations, explicit tool choice, and replayed function calls/results. Upstream calls are mapped back before caller catalog resolution, so the caller still receives and executes collaboration tools. This is a copy-on-write transport transform: it does not change the caller request, tool arguments, other schemas, or encrypted output metadata. Ordinary Responses API routes retain the original namespace.

Collaboration tool arguments. The three caller tools collaboration.spawn_agent, collaboration.send_message, and collaboration.followup_task are emitted with encrypted_function_args: [] when their provider-neutral arguments are plaintext. This is an explicit Codex transport marker, not a content heuristic, and appears on the added, arguments-done, final item, and final response snapshot. Other tools are unchanged. When a Responses upstream supplies an encrypted_function_args string array, the gateway preserves it opaquely instead; it never decrypts it or relabels it as plaintext. Metadata supplied at an added boundary is validated there and must match the later completed item or final snapshot; an early call that omits the field may still supply it at completion. Malformed upstream metadata fails the provider output.

Response ids, cache affinity, and turn state

Response ids. Every response id is resp_<32 hex>. While the usage ledger is on (diagnostics), responses from Copilot and Claude subscription routes use resp_gl_<request id without dashes>, the same hex as the X-Request-Id header. Usage and billing detail (cache writes, reasoning tokens, Copilot credits) stay in the local ledger and never appear in the response.

Codex sends a prompt_cache_key in the body and session-id and thread-id headers. The body key passes through unchanged. For the ChatGPT subscription provider, the gateway also forwards those two headers. Without them, that endpoint did not reuse its prompt cache: identical 27k-token requests stayed at 0 cached tokens. With them, repeats were 99.5% cached. Only well-formed identifiers of at most 128 characters are forwarded. Official OpenCode API routes also receive the caller's thread or session ID as x-opencode-session, along with the gateway's user agent, across all three API transports. Other Responses endpoints receive only the body key, except official OpenRouter routes, which also receive their documented x-session-id affinity header. See API providers.

The subscription endpoint also returns x-codex-turn-state on a new turn (about 780 characters, verified live), which Codex echoes on the following requests of that turn to keep it on the same backend. The gateway returns it to Codex wrapped with a per-account scope, and forwards it upstream only when the scope matches the same account route. Values from another route, malformed values and upstream values over 6000 characters are dropped; none is ever logged. For a streaming request to the Codex 2 route, the response head waits for the provider's first event so it can carry the header, because a streaming response cannot add a header later. The provider reports that event as soon as the upstream response head arrives, which took between 1.5 and 4.7 seconds in live checks. The wait lasts at most one heartbeat interval (15 seconds) after admission, the same silence an open stream allows before a progress event; a request that has to queue opens its head at once. request_completed and request_failed record only whether a turn-state was echoed and returned.

Service tiers on Responses upstreams

Responses upstreams retain service_tier. For Codex subscription requests, the fast alias becomes priority, as required by the tested subscription resource endpoint. Declared model capabilities reject unsupported tiers before inference. Standard requests omit a null tier; explicit default and auto keep their wire values. A successful completion reports the upstream's actual service_tier only when it is a recognized public value. It never reports the requested tier as proof of the tier served. An upstream may return default after a priority request; the gateway preserves that result and does not retry to chase Fast.

Per-provider tiers, including how flex and Fast are mapped on the Claude and Copilot routes, are on Responses provider adapters and images.

Replayed items and turn terminals

Codex also replays agent_message items: text one agent wrote to another, with its encrypted transport state beside it. The public Responses endpoint the gateway uses rejects agent_message items (HTTP 400, verified), unlike the native Codex backend, so every route, Responses upstreams included, receives one user-role message whose text is the item's input_text and output_text parts joined in order; encrypted parts contribute nothing, and an item with no text adds no message. Author and recipient are never rendered into the transcript as labels or prose. Any other part type, including an image, fails as a client error before a provider is invoked.

Responses upstream completion retains an actual boolean end_turn when present. An absent value remains absent. This lets the SDK distinguish a continuation from the end of a turn, including a response containing only caller tools. Assistant message boundaries and supplied commentary, final_answer, or partial_answer phases are retained. Actual text found in an output-item or final snapshot fills only a confirmed unstreamed suffix; repeated snapshots cannot duplicate text or execute a tool twice. Conflicting identities, phases, or text prefixes fail explicitly instead of silently discarding content. An actual response.incomplete with reason interrupted retains that terminal, its incomplete message statuses, and end_turn: false. The SDK can continue the same user turn with the supplied history. Unfinished tool arguments are never dispatched. A completed terminal cannot discard an unfinished tool call; a genuine completed call must resolve it first. Other incomplete reasons remain failures. A minimal actual response.completed with a valid response ID is accepted when its status field is absent, matching the tested SDK contract.

Streaming, reasoning summaries, and heartbeats

Text streams through Responses SSE as the provider emits it. Tool arguments are returned when the native call is complete. Claude's thinking events and Codex's reasoning summaries use Responses reasoning-summary events. An effort setting does not guarantee that a provider emits reasoning on every request. The gateway does not invent reasoning. Claude's native thinking signatures are not replayed; Codex's opaque encrypted reasoning state is wrapped with its account route and restored only on that route. Switching providers or accounts retains readable summaries and drops incompatible opaque state. Claude CLI replay preserves their reasoning-summary identity instead of relabeling them as ordinary assistant speech; other translating routes retain their existing text representation. Untagged reasoning imported from another client also retains only its readable summary. Use a new provider ID and credential file for a new account. Generated Codex settings explicitly request model_reasoning_summary = "auto". The client can set it to none to hide provider reasoning. For Responses upstreams, none removes the summary field on the wire and hides text summaries locally. Opaque replay state remains available on its account route. Newer Claude models omit thinking text unless asked. When thinking is on and the summary is not none, the adapter starts the CLI with --thinking-display summarized, so long Max turns stream readable reasoning. When the CLI still reports only token progress, the gateway emits empty summary deltas with an estimated_tokens extension instead of fabricating a summary.

Gateway authentication, capacity, and request-validation failures return HTTP errors. A validated streaming request emits response.created before waiting for the provider. During a quiet period, genuine response.in_progress data events keep the Codex connection alive every fifteen seconds. They retain the response identity and sequence and contain no invented text or completion. Heartbeats stop on completion, failure, disconnect, or deadline.

Provider failures and retry budgets

Provider failures emit response.failed, including failures before the first output delta. Nonstream requests retain the corresponding HTTP error status. Responses upstream context_length_exceeded errors keep that code so Codex's compaction recovery can trim history and retry. The gateway does not choose a different model or account. Chat Completions servers such as vLLM report the same overflow as a plain HTTP 400 whose message says "maximum context length is N tokens", with no code. The gateway maps that message to context_length_exceeded too, keeping only the token counts, so a long local Qwen chat compacts instead of resending the same oversized request until it fails. Other 400s keep their ordinary classification. Transport failures and deadline expiry have separate messages; they do not imply a failed login. Responses upstream server errors retry once after one second only before any text, reasoning state, or tool output has been published. Known transient connection failures before output, including socket resets and temporary DNS failures, get their own budget instead: the gateway waits one second, then two, four and eight seconds per retry (each within twenty percent of jitter) for up to 120 seconds, so a short outage is absorbed here rather than ending the chat. No attempt starts at or after that deadline: a wait that would cross it is refused, and the deadline is checked again after an abortable wait in case sleep or an event-loop stall overshot it; the triggering failure is returned unchanged. An attempt already in flight may finish after its retry window; the caller deadline remains its bound. The budget is timed from the first connection failure, so a throttle earlier in the request cannot spend it. The stream keeps sending its heartbeat while the provider has produced nothing, so the wait stays covered. Every other retryable class keeps the single retry above, whichever attempt it lands on. A connection failure after any inference output is not replayed. Certificate failures, permanent DNS failures, refused connections, unknown network faults, OAuth refresh failures, and cancellations receive no additional internal retry. A clean EOF without a terminal event has the same single retry only before any inference output has been published. Cancellation stops that wait. Quota, authentication, malformed streams, partial responses, and unclassified stream failures other than an error or response.failed event with an unknown code never retry automatically. EOF and [DONE] never substitute for a genuine Responses terminal.

Chat Completions routes (including Qwen over the checked tailnet transport) use the same 120-second connection budget while acquiring an HTTP response. Each retry preserves the model, account, request and routing headers, and rechecks the tailnet destination. Only allowlisted transient connection failures qualify; HTTP replies, certificate errors, permanent DNS failures, address refusals, unknown faults and cancellation do not. Once any HTTP response arrives, its body is consumed exactly once: a disconnect after headers, buffered tool fragments, usage or partial output never enters this retry loop. The existing opt-in Messages empty-completion recovery remains separate. As with Responses connection retries, a failure before HTTP headers does not prove the upstream never accepted the request. A retry can repeat computation whose usage was never reported; this is transport recovery, not an exactly-once inference guarantee.

Private failure logs contain a UTC timestamp, bounded request/provider/model identifiers, elapsed time, error code, and status, excluding request bodies, exception messages, stacks, and credentials. Failed Responses streams retain allowlisted upstream error codes, event types, and request IDs. Missing-terminal EOF records include only event counts, an allowlisted last event, reasoning add/done event counts, text-delta counts, and distinct dispatched tool-call counts. HTTP 500/502/503/504 failures have the same single retry before output. An HTTP 429 is a throttle when its error.code or error.type names a temporary rate limit (for example rate_limit_exceeded, rate_limit_error or limit_requests), or when it names no quota class and asks for a Retry-After of at most 60 seconds. On a Responses route, a throttle (an HTTP 429 throttle or a stream error naming a temporary rate limit) has its own retry budget before output, separate from the connection budget and from the single retry of other classes. The gateway waits one, two, four and then eight seconds per retry, jittered by ±20%, or a provider's Retry-After of at least one second, for up to 120 seconds from the first throttle. The 60-second header rule applies only to an otherwise unnamed 429; a named temporary throttle may use the remaining 120-second budget. It never starts a wait that would end past the budget, and checks again after the abortable wait before it starts the next request; an already-started request remains bounded by the caller deadline. The ChatGPT backend usually throttles without Retry-After and for longer than Codex's own retry schedule (about 10 seconds), so earlier releases, which retried once after one second, failed the turn while the throttle was still active. When the budget runs out, the throttle returns as rate_limit_exceeded (HTTP 429) with the message "Provider is temporarily rate limiting requests; retry shortly" and stays retryable for Codex. A 429 that names a quota, billing, spend or plan class (such as insufficient_quota or usage_limit_reached), and any other 429, is a final usage limit. ChatGPT reports a shared subscription that has used its allowance as subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded, with the generic type invalid_request_error, either in a 429 body or in a stream error and response.failed event. That code is a final usage limit too, and the message says the ChatGPT account reached its usage limit. Earlier releases treated it as an unknown stream failure, so Codex retried five times and showed a stream disconnect. Cancellation and the request deadline bound all backoff waits; no quota or account switch is attempted.

timeoutMs (ten minutes by default) bounds silence, not total length. It covers the upload and queue wait, then restarts at admission and on every provider event, so a long Max or Ultra stream continues while a stalled provider still fails. Every request also has a one-hour cap. Disconnects abort inference and release capacity.

Codex keeps its own stream retry policy. The gateway sets Codex's stream idle timeout to 90 seconds, independent of timeoutMs, because healthy streams receive progress every 15 seconds; a dead path fails in 90 seconds instead of freezing the turn. Failures that would repeat identically (invalid request or JSON, unknown model, oversized request, unsupported protocol, authentication) are reported inside a stream with Codex's non-retryable invalid_prompt code and the gateway's message, so Codex stops at once instead of retrying five times. Codex ends a failed turn without a final answer and does not save the error in the chat transcript, so a client that reconnects later sees only the ended turn. Claude failures without a native error code record the CLI's allowlisted result subtype, such as error_max_turns. A usage limit or exhausted credit balance is final: Codex receives it as invalid_prompt and stops instead of retrying five times (verified: one upstream request instead of six). An HTTP 429 throttle, as defined above, stays retryable on every HTTP route, including the Anthropic API and Chat Completions servers, so per-minute API limits still clear by themselves. A Claude rate limit without a rejected rate_limit_event, and a Copilot error that names a rate limit without usage-limit or quota wording, are retryable throttles too. Responses streams recognize explicit usage, credit, quota, and billing classes in either the upstream error's code or type. A named quota takes precedence over a temporary rate-limit class. HTTP quota failures retain the allowlisted class, HTTP status, and validated request ID for diagnostics too. Exhausted credits report "Provider credits or quota are exhausted"; a subscription usage limit reports "Provider usage limit reached". Private upstream error prose is never shown. Upstream rejections that would repeat identically (invalid_prompt, invalid_encrypted_content, cyber_policy, bio_policy, misalignment_policy_violation, usage_not_included), from a stream or an HTTP body, become upstream_rejected with a fixed message per class. A recognized refusal in error.type is retained even beside a generic error.code. The subscription_sharing_unsupported_capability refusal also becomes final, with guidance to use a supported gateway tool or native Codex instead of retrying the same request. These classifications do not bypass provider policy, grant capabilities, or change subscription allowances. The sharing-limit message names gateway subscription sharing; it does not establish the native account's remaining allowance. Diagnostics keep the exact upstream code and HTTP status. content_filter, max_output_tokens and unknown stream codes stay retryable, as they are in native Codex. A body code such as server_is_overloaded marks a transient failure only in a stream; an HTTP 4xx is never retried for it. Codex receives those rejections as their own code when it is one of Codex's final codes, and as invalid_prompt otherwise; an HTTP 400, 404, 413 or 422 from an upstream also becomes invalid_prompt. Timeouts, upstream_unavailable and rate limits stay retryable.

Capacity and supported surface

The daemon runs at most maxConcurrent providers (four by default). Up to 32 additional requests wait in a FIFO queue instead of receiving immediate capacity errors. Waiting streams receive the same progress events; their deadline includes waiting time. Cancellation removes waiting work without invoking a provider. The admission bound includes body uploads. A full queue returns busy with HTTP 429 and Retry-After: 1. Health exposes running and queued counts.

The current adapters support text, inline images, and caller-dispatched tools. Audio input, hosted tools, previous-response-ID state, and every provider's full option surface are not supported. This is not a claim of complete Responses API compatibility.

WebSocket refusals, internal fields, and control items

The gateway serves /v1/responses over plain HTTP only. A WebSocket (or any other) upgrade attempt to /v1/responses with a valid bearer gets HTTP/1.1 426 Upgrade Required with no body and Connection: close. The checks run in this order: a request target that cannot be parsed (GET http://[ HTTP/1.1) gets 400; a request with an Origin header gets 403; a missing or wrong bearer gets 401; an upgrade to any other path gets 404. The refusal runs in the server's upgrade listener. On Node builds that pass upgrades to the request handler instead, that handler gives an upgrade to /v1/responses the same checks and the same 426, and serves an upgrade to any other path as an ordinary request; there a request counts as an upgrade only when Connection names the upgrade token beside an Upgrade header, as Node's own parser requires, so a POST with Upgrade: h2c is served normally. It never admits a request, changes the health admission counters, or invokes a provider.

The upgrade listener closes the socket as soon as the refusal is flushed, and after two seconds at the latest if the client never reads it. A server accepts half-open sockets and applies no timeout once a request has asked for an upgrade, so a client that keeps its side open would otherwise hold the socket, and the server's close() with it, until the process ends.

An unreadable request target on an ordinary request also gets 400 (invalid_request). If the request handler fails in a way nothing else caught, the client gets 500 (internal_error) while the response head is unsent, or the connection is cut once it is not. The failure is reported as a scrubbed exception and never ends the process.

Recent Codex builds carry internal transport state beside the conversation. Before translation or any provider sees a request, the gateway removes it once in the request handler: internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough from every input item, encrypted_function_args from function_call items (their plaintext arguments stay), and mcp_attribution from client_metadata; every other client_metadata key passes through untouched. When nothing is removed the parsed body is forwarded as the same object, so Responses upstreams receive byte-identical requests to before the strip existed. The strip covers every route, including a Messages request after it has been translated. Shapes that are not objects (client_metadata that is null, an array or a string, an input item that is null, a number or an array) are not read as maps and are left for translation to accept or reject.

Codex app builds from 26.1103 send client context, such as codex_apps_open_page page snapshots, as a function_call_output with a name and no call_id. It answers no tool call, so the request handler rewrites it once, for every route, as a user message whose text is <external_NAME>OUTPUT</external_NAME>, the form the app itself presents to models. Outputs that carry a call_id are unchanged. The count is contextOutputs.

Two input items are executor control, not model input. A configuration_update item is removed before translation and counted in the request's telemetry record as droppedControlItems (a count only, never item content). A compaction_trigger item fails the request as final: streams get a response.failed with Codex's non-retryable invalid_prompt code and the fixed message "This gateway serves compaction inside the gateway executor; this Codex build sent remote compaction, which the gateway does not support yet."; nonstream requests get HTTP 400 invalid_request with that message. request_failed records translation_reason: unsupported_compaction, and the stderr provider_failure line and gateway diagnostics carry it too (diagnostics). Neither invokes a provider nor takes an admission slot, and the refusal is final. A gateway at capacity (the larger of top-level maxConcurrent and the sum of effective provider limits, plus 32 requests in flight) answers every inference request (/v1/responses and /v1/messages) with a retryable 429 before reading its body, so an overload never buffers bodies; a compaction refused that way is retried and gets this final refusal once a slot is free.

/health adds features: ["responses-ws-426", "openai-internal-strip", "native-identity-v1"], the behaviors this release guarantees (the exported gatewayFeatures), so an operator can tell an updated daemon from an old one without reading its code. responses-ws-426 is the WebSocket refusal above. openai-internal-strip is the removal of internal fields and control items. native-identity-v1 means this inference server accepts requests from a gateway executor that runs under the native openai provider identity: the two behaviors above, which such an executor needs, are both present. It describes the server only; whether executors run under that identity is a separate setting of the desktop adapter (chatIdentity, gatefox by default; subscription_gateway before 1.8.0). Since 0.4.7 executors reach this server through the gateway's own provider definition even for chats recorded as openai, so they do not depend on these two behaviors; see harness identity.
